Chapter 4: Practical Tools for Countering Bias and Improving Decisions.
So, we've talked about the science behind better decision-making, but let's be honest—real change doesn't happen until you’ve got practical tools you can actually use every day.
These tools are all about turning theory into action, helping you and your team spot bias, put your assumptions to the test, and feel more confident in the choices you make.
One of the best ways to do this? Structured checklists.
Think about how pilots use checklists before every flight—to make sure nothing critical gets missed. In the same way, you can use a decision checklist to keep your process on track.
For example, your checklist could include questions like:
Have all the right people been consulted?
What evidence do we actually have for each option?
Are there any red flags—like overconfidence or groupthink—showing up?
And what about possible unintended consequences?
By spelling out these questions, checklists make sure you don’t overlook something important just because you’re in a hurry or feeling pressure to act fast.
Now, here’s another powerful tool: the “premortem” exercise.
Instead of waiting until a project crashes and then asking what went wrong, why not imagine the worst has already happened?
Work backwards and ask, “What could’ve led us here?”
This isn’t about being negative—it’s about surfacing hidden risks and getting people to talk openly about what might go wrong, before it actually does.
Encouraging dissent and diversity of thought is just as important.
If everyone in the group is thinking the same way, you’re probably missing something.
Leaders can shake things up by assigning someone to play devil’s advocate, specifically to question assumptions and spot risks.
Or, invite input from folks with different backgrounds or expertise.
And make it a point to reward people who raise concerns, instead of shutting them down.
Scenario planning is another great approach.
Map out a few different futures: the best case, the worst case, and what’s most likely. By doing this, your team is better prepared for surprises and less likely to get caught off guard by the unexpected.
Finally, let’s talk about reflection and feedback.
Once you’ve made a decision and put it into action, take time to review how things turned out.
What worked? What didn’t? And most importantly, what can you tweak moving forward?
This kind of regular review builds a culture where learning and improvement are just part of how you do business.
Remember, these tools aren’t here to replace your judgment—they’re here to sharpen it.
Think of them as guardrails, keeping your decisions on track and helping you avoid the pitfalls of bias.
Use them consistently, and you’ll start to see decision-making become less about luck or gut instinct, and more about a clear, disciplined process you and your team can rely on.
